query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-oxidizing a thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coating at moderate high temperatures promotes selective Cu segregation to grain boundaries, leading to the in situ formation of a continuous, thin, and adherent oxide layer that effectively reduces high‐temperature wear by acting as a protective barrier against asperity contact and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate with a controlled grain size and uniform composition.
generation.intervention: Apply a pre-oxidation treatment at approximately 450°C for a controlled duration in a controlled atmosphere to trigger selective Cu segregation and initiate formation of a uniform, thin oxide layer along the grain boundaries before wear testing.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear tests conducted at temperatures between 400°C and 600°C under mechanical loads representative of industrial or automotive protective coating applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and stabilization of a fine, continuous oxide scale—especially along the grain boundaries—mediated by selective Cu segregation.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated oxidation during the pre-treatment promotes Cu segregation at grain boundaries, resulting in the formation of a self-healing, adherent oxide film that reduces direct asperity contact during mechanical wear. This oxide film acts as a diffusion barrier and strain moderator, thereby lowering wear rates even under cyclic high-temperature loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline untreated coating, the pre-oxidized coating should exhibit a lower friction coefficient, reduced wear rate, and microstructural evidence (via TEM/SEM) of a continuous, thin and adherent oxide film, particularly concentrated at grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: An untreated FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating subjected directly to high-temperature wear tests without any pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only to thin protective coatings (not bulk materials) used in high-temperature regimes (400°C to 600°C) under relevant mechanical loading conditions. It may not hold at different temperature ranges or if the coating thickness/grain size deviates significantly.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of the improvement in wear resistance (i.e., exact percentage reduction in wear rate or friction coefficient) remains uncertain and may depend on the precise pre-oxidation parameters and microstructural variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on conventional metal substrates: one set receives the pre-oxidation treatment at 450°C in a controlled atmosphere, and the other set remains untreated. Subject both sets to identical wear tests under high-temperature conditions (400°C to 600°C) and comparable mechanical loads.
measurements: Wear rate measurement (e.g., mass loss per unit area)
Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) to analyze oxide layer continuity, thickness, and grain boundary coverage
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in wear rate and friction coefficient compared to the untreated coatings, or if microstructural analysis shows no notable difference in the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide layer along grain boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. frame.system: FeNiCrCoCu used as a thin-film protective coating on conventional metal substrates, with a microstructure featuring controlled grain size and composition tailored for oxidation and wear performance.
frame.goal: To explain and predict the overall wear resistance under high‐temperature conditions by identifying the mechanistic role of thermally activated processes (e.g., grain boundary oxidation and phase stability) during wear.
frame.limitation: Prior studies have focused mainly on room-temperature or limited thermal conditions, examining the alloy’s intrinsic properties (grain size, composition, substrate interface) without addressing the complete wear response of the coating at high temperatures.

frame.regime: High-temperature wear conditions, for example, operating from 400°C to 600°C under applied mechanical loads representative of service conditions in industrial or automotive applications.
prior_attempts: Earlier studies assessed wear behavior at room temperature or within limited thermal ranges, focusing primarily on the alloy, its grain size, and composition, rather than investigating the full coupling of thermal and mechanical effects in a coating–substrate system.
frame.understanding: Under high-temperature wear conditions, the primary mechanism governing the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu coatings is the formation and stability of a fine, adherent, and self-healing oxide layer at the coating surface and along grain boundaries. This oxide layer, which forms due to thermally activated oxidation processes, can act as a protective barrier that reduces direct asperity contact and mediates strain accommodation. However, if the oxide layer is too thick or spalls off due to poor adherence, wear resistance will decline. The hypothesis posits that an intervention involving a pre-oxidation treatment engineered to modify grain boundary chemistry (e.g., slight enrichment in Cu or controlled heat-treatment to promote a more uniform initial oxide film) will stabilize the oxide formation process. Compared to a baseline untreated coating, the treated coating will exhibit a more uniform and adherent oxidized grain-boundary network that resists wear better under high-temperature loading. Observations that support the hypothesis would include microstructural evidence (via TEM/SEM analysis) of a continuous, thin oxide layer, lower friction coefficients, and reduced wear rates in mechanical tests at 400°C to 600°C. Conversely, the hypothesis would be falsified if, upon intervention, the microstructure shows no significant difference in oxide scale formation, or if the wear resistance metrics (e.g., wear rate, friction coefficient) do not statistically improve compared to the baseline coating under the specified test conditions.

decision.trend: Initial studies of HEA coatings at elevated temperatures (e.g., the AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 system in PMC7515071) revealed that at high temperatures, the formation of a fine, adherent oxide (such as a spinel phase) can sharply reduce wear by limiting direct asperity contact and accommodating local strain. These works first characterized the intrinsic alloy properties and microstructural evolution under thermal loading, yet they did not systematically tune the coating’s grain boundary chemistry to harness the benefits of a controlled oxide scale in the complete coating–substrate system.
decision.unsolved: It remains unaddressed how a targeted pre‐oxidation treatment that modifies grain boundary chemistry (e.g., via selective Cu segregation) can be used to pre-establish a uniform, self-healing and thin oxide layer that effectively governs wear resistance across the high-temperature regime under realistic loads.
decision.lever: Apply a pre-oxidation treatment at around 450°C for a controlled duration in a controlled atmosphere to promote selective segregation of Cu at grain boundaries and induce the formation of a continuous, thin oxide film prior to wear testing
decision.why: This intervention directly leverages trends observed in high-temperature oxidation studies: coating performance improves with a protective oxide that forms in situ. By pre-engineering the oxide via thermal treatment, the experiment tests whether a uniform, adherent oxide can reduce friction and wear under high-temperature loads (400–600°C). This approach fills the gap between alloy-centric studies and coating–substrate wear response and aligns with the niche move calling for high-temperature wear testing combined with surface chemical and microstructural analysis.
